analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over leasing and permitting for oil and gas drilling on federal land, bypassing federal environmental reviews.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let a state take over from the federal government the leasing, permitting, and regulation of oil, gas, and other energy development on federal land inside that state. Once a state made that declaration, its actions would no longer be considered federal actions, so they would be exempt from the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and federal administrative review. Royalties would still be collected at the federal level and deposited in federal accounts, and parks, wildlife refuges, and designated wilderness areas would be excluded. The bill never received a committee hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that want to drill on federal land would be the main beneficiaries: they would get state permitting instead of federal permitting, which the bill's own findings say took 197 days on average in 2013, and the permits would no longer be subject to Endangered Species Act or National Environmental Policy Act review, reducing the chance of delays or lawsuits. States with oil and gas programs would gain regulatory authority and could charge companies their own processing fees. Federal taxpayers would keep the same royalty revenue, since the bill requires states to collect royalties at the same level and deposit them in the same federal accounts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: States with oil and gas regulatory programs could declare their intent and immediately take over leasing, permitting, and regulation of all oil, gas, and energy development on federal land in the state, with no federal approval required.
By exempting state actions from federal permitting and environmental laws, it would speed up drilling approvals that today can take months of federal review and litigation.
It reserves National Parks, Wildlife Refuges, and designated wilderness, so state control would apply to other available federal land.

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on the public interest in federally owned land: fewer legal checks on drilling near endangered species habitat, historic sites, and other lands owned by all Americans, since state permitting decisions would not be reviewable as federal actions. Because royalties still flow to the Treasury, the public does not gain revenue from the transfer of control.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via weakened federal land safeguards

drawbacks.text: It removes Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act review for oil and gas development on federal land, so projects that threaten listed species or significant environmental harm could proceed without the federal environmental analysis that applies today.

Because state actions would not count as federal actions, federal environmental review under the Administrative Procedure Act would also be unavailable, leaving no hearing or legal check on how a state approves drilling on land owned by all Americans.

A state could take over leasing on federal land within its borders with no federal sign-off required, raising concerns about whether states would manage land held in trust for the whole nation in the public's interest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's own stated aims—faster permitting and domestic energy production—would likely be achieved, since state review is generally quicker than federal review with environmental lawsuits. But the cost is real and one-sided: it removes the only checks (Endangered Species Act and NEPA) that apply to drilling on land owned by all Americans, and the hearing procedure exempts the public from the process entirely. Revenues stay with the Treasury, so the public does not even gain from state control; the oil and gas industry gains permitting speed while bearing none of the process burdens. For a bill whose beneficiaries are concentrated and whose costs fall on shared public resources, the drawbacks outweigh the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Inhofe introduced the bill on July 20, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no vote on the bill and the full Senate never considered it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal environmental oversight stays intact, since the bill never moved; no state gained control over federal land and no environmental protections were removed.

for.name: James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in this Congress.

for.name: 7 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Capito, Cruz, Cramer, Lummis, Lankford, Crapo, plus Inhofe)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Republicans.

for.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out, keeping it from a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill received no Democratic support in the record.

industries.note: The bill would hand oil and gas companies a faster permitting path on federal land, free of the Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act, which today can slow or block projects. The federal royalties are preserved, so the industry's main gain is speed and fewer legal obstacles.

industries.industry: State oil and gas regulatory agencies
industries.note: States would become the permanent gatekeepers for energy development on federal land in their borders, a large expansion of their authority. State agencies would collect their own administrative fees, and their decisions would be immune from federal environmental review.
